#  The mediating effects of engagement on the relationship between perceived digital inquiry and creativity

##  Introduction

Individuals’ perceptions of their creativity are considered to have significant effects on improve- ments in their creative performance, problem-solving, and academic achievement (Anderson & Haney, 2021; Zhou et al., 2014). As creativity is a critical learning outcome of STEM education (Weng, Chiu, & Jong, 2022; Honey et al., 2014), we regard STEM learning as a potential envi- ronment that cultivates the factors associated with student creativity. For instance, in the context of STEM learning, students’ self-related factors including perceived digital inquiry and engagement with learning tasks are essential agents of creativity development (de Jong et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2020). Fostering this development requires the process of intentionally gaining new insights and different ideas through existing information (Pande & Bharathi, 2020). In the process, stu- dents feel empowered to develop more ideas when embedding digital technologies into STEM education (Weng, Cui, et al., 2022; Weng, Chiu, & Tsang, 2022 ).

The digital technologies create more authentic learning and assessment and can better engage students in inquiry-based learning (Lindgren, & Johnson-Glenberg, 2013). For example, the students who perceive stronger self-efficacy in using digital tools for inquiry-based learning (referred to as perceived digital inquiry) are likely to have more new ideas and feel they can create something new. Moreover, student engagement is the key to creativity development in STEM education (Weng, Chiu, & Tsang, 2022). Student engagement is multifaceted with major dimensions including behavioral, emotional, and cognitive. Emotional and cognitive engagement are relatively more influential on student creativity development (Orkibi & Ram-Vlasov, 2019 ). Students engaging in fun and interesting learning environments (i.e., emotional engagement) are more curious, and always want to learn and see STEM problems from multiple perspectives (Gallagher & Grimm, 2018). Students who are willing and able to take on challenges (cognitive engagement) keep improving their ideas when solving STEM problems (Guan et al., 2021 ).

Accordingly, how students perceive their digital inquiry competence, and emotional and cognitive engagement in learning could affect their creative thinking in STEM education. It is necessary to understand how these factors relate to creativity. This gap is supported by recent studies advocating that student perceptions of digital inquiry, emotional engagement, and cog- nitive engagement have received growing attention in STEM education research (Händel et al., 2022; Howard et al., 2016). However, most of the engagement-related previous studies in STEM education used the different dimensions of student engagement as the final outcomes (Chiu, [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Hall & Miro, 2016; Struyf et al., 2019). Very few studies used emotional and cognitive engagement as mediators. Furthermore, most related studies that have investigated perceived competencies and engagement were conducted in higher education or non-interdisciplinary contexts (Yang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014). Student engagement is an important mediator in adolescent learning (Chiu, [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2022)](#disclosure-statement). Therefore, the generalizability of the findings of these studies to STEM learning in K-12 settings merits exploration (Lawson & Lawson, 2013 ).

The transactional model of engagement (TME) offers a framework to explain the relationships between various perceived competencies that lead to and benefit from engagement acts (Lawson & Lawson, 2013). Accordingly, this study investigates creativity in digital learning environments through STEM school education from a different perspective—student engagement as mediators. It uses the TME as the theoretical framework to (i) investigate the direct associations between perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity and (ii) examine the mediating effects of emotional and cognitive engagement on the association between perceived digital inquiry and creativity.

## The proposed research model

This section explains what the TME is and proposes a research model with hypotheses.

### _The TME framework and engagement-related studies_

The TME framework provides a transactional view of student engagement. In this view, the engagement process consists of four main components. They are acts of engagement, benefits of engagement, dispositions for engagement, and conditions/contexts of engagement. Each of these components is linked by a temporal dimension. First, act of engagement refers to the various states of experience of individuals. It states how students’ experiences lead to their states such as joy, fun, boredom, and disinterest (Bempechat & Shernoff, 2012; Pekrun & Linnenbrink-Garcia, 2012). This component includes behavioral, cognitive and emotional engage- ment. Second, the idea of benefits of engagement refers to the outcomes of engagement-related acts. The quality of experiences directly determines whether students receive the benefits from each of the acts. The benefits are seen as student proximal outcomes; they are either obscure or solid, such as feelings, belongings, competencies, academic achievements, and participation. Third, the notion of dispositions for engagement refers to students’ perceptions of the “will” and “skill” they bring to an activity, including motivation, interests, self-directed learning, and language proficiency. Students’ prior learning experiences are influential factors important to these perceptions (Taines, 2012). Finally, an engagement disposition is developmental, which is highly influenced by engagement’s surrounding conditions, cultures, and contexts. These ideas are conditions/contexts of engagement. Lawson and Lawson (2013) state that the TME is a new and contemporary conceptual framework for student engagement research and practice.

K-12 students are adolescents, and their engagement is the key to their STEM learning as its multifaceted nature affects their outcomes in different ways. However, most of the engagement-related studies use the different dimensions of engagement as final outcomes, particularly in STEM edu- cation (Chiu, [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Hall & Miro, 2016; Struyf et al., 2019). Very few used different dimensions of engagement as mediators explaining relations between perceived competencies and learning outcomes. This gap can be addressed by the TME. As in the current study, participants

### had a similar social-cultural background and the learning context, and the research goal focuses on specific constructs representing the first three engagement components and their connections. Based on the TME, we propose that positively perceived digital inquiry competencies can trigger and encourage students’ emotional and cognitive engagement, leading to engagement benefits from the positive affect associated with stronger self-perceived creativity, see Figure 1. The following defines each of the constructs and discusses the proposed research model for this study.

##  _Perceived digital inquiry_

Perceived digital inquiry is defined as students’ perceptions of their competencies in using digital tools to conduct inquiry activities in various learning contexts (de Jong et al., 2021). Some STEM education studies have suggested that students tend to perceive stronger digital inquiry when they have opportunities to explore or interact with technological tools (Bruce & Casey, 2012; de Jong et al., 2021). Perceiving stronger digital inquiry usually implies successful interactions or experiences with digital learning environments, resulting in more positive dispositions toward learning institutions such as schools (Porat et al., 2018). According to the TME, perceived digital inquiry can be regarded as an engagement disposition that fosters students’ acts of engagement (Lawson & Lawson, 2013).

## _Emotional and cognitive engagement_

In the TME, acts of engagement indicate the various states that students can experience, from flow-like experiences to feelings of boredom or disinterest, as they participate in learning activities (Lawson & Lawson, 2013). This study focuses on acts of emotional engagement and cognitive engagement, which are crucial psychological resources for student learning (Pietarinen et al., 2014 ). Emotional engagement concerns individuals’ affection during learning activities, which involves both positive and negative emotions (Ninaus et al., 2019). Cognitive engagement reflects students’ willingness to make efforts to understand learning content and master skills (Li et al., 2021 ). These two types of engagement interact with each other (Chiu, [2021 ,](#disclosure-statement) [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2022 ;](#disclosure-statement)  Dubovi & Tabak, 2021; Hong et al., 2020). Moreover, they are significant resources that facilitate the creative process of student learning (Álvarez-Huerta et al., [2021;](#disclosure-statement) Sun, 2020). As creativity is a major out- come of STEM activities (Honey et al., 2014), emotional engagement and cognitive engagement have received increasing research attention in STEM-related areas (Fredricks et al., 2018 ). 

##  _Perceived creativity_

Studies have categorized creativity in terms of two constructs: self-perceptions of creativity (i.e., perceived creativity; Silvia et al., 2012) and domain-specific creativity (i.e., creativity performance; Barbot, 2020). Perceived creativity refers to the creative skills that students believe they possess. This perception indicates how learners think of their abilities to generate ideas that are inno- vative and useful (Kaufman et al., 2016; Laguía et al., 2019). Kaufman ( 2019), Laguía et al. (2019 ), and Silvia et al. (2012) suggested that perceived creativity can foster creative performance. Correlations have been found between students’ self-beliefs about their creativity and their 

434 X. WENG AND T. K. F. CHIU

divergent thinking, self-rated creativity, and self-reported creative activities (Chiu, [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Kaufman et al., 2016). Because of the significance of perceived creativity, it was chosen as the measured outcome of engagement acts in this study.

Two types of self-rated factors that influence individuals’ judgments about their efforts and accomplishments relating to creativity have been identified (Kaufman et al., 2016). The first concerns being aware of one’s own strengths and weaknesses related to creativity, both within a specific area (e.g., perceived digital inquiry) and as a general attribute. The other concerns knowing when, where, how, and why to be creative by considering the social contextual interplay (i.e., engagement interactions with the learning tasks). Both self-rated factors interact with each other in the development of creativity (Fischer et al., 2019; Richter et al., 2012 ). Therefore, research on perceived creativity should simultaneously consider these two factors. In this study, we emphasize the interactions between the two self-rated factors by examining how perceived digital inquiry and emotional and cognitive engagement with learning tasks explain perceived creativity in STEM learning.

## _Relationships between perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity_

Studies have reported associations between perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity. Perceived digital inquiry has been shown to have large positive direct effects on students’ emotional and cognitive engagement (Marty et al., 2013 ; Wu & Wu, 2020). For instance, a survey-based study of 605 secondary school students in Taiwan revealed that the students’ perceptions of their inquiry-related characteristics (e.g., curiosity) were associated with different dimensions of engagement in a technology-facilitated science laboratory context (Wu & Wu, 2020).

Many studies have demonstrated that emotional engagement and cognitive engagement are related bidirectionally. For instance, Chiu et al. ([2012)](#disclosure-statement) analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) data of immigrant children in 41 countries and reported that the cognitive and emotional components of the students’ engagement were interconnected. Dubovi and Tabak (2021) analyzed 14,700 trending YouTube videos about science topics and found that the public’s emotional engagement and cognitive engagement in learning science via social media were interrelated. Additionally, Hong et al. (2020) conducted a study of 789 Chinese primary school students in which they distributed a mathematics engagement scale three times over a 1.5-year intervention. Their findings suggest that students’ cognitive and emotional engagement influences each other over time.

Moreover, perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, and cognitive engagement have direct impacts on students’ self-perceived creativity. Some scholars have provided evidence that students’ perceived digital inquiry and creativity are positively associated. For example, Hwang et al. (2018) collected the perceptions of 658 high school students from Taiwan and found a positive relationship between the students’ inquiry-related use of mobile phones and learning behaviors and their tendency to engage in creativity. Furthermore, many researchers have reported a positive relationship between students’ engagement and perceived creativity. Wang et al. (2022 ) surveyed 542 postgraduate students in China and found that learning engagement involving both emotional and cognitive components had a positive effect on the respondents’ self-reported creativity. Similarly, in a study of 775 Spanish university students, Álvarez-Huerta et al. ([2021)](#disclosure-statement) investigated the association between the participants’ engagement, which had a cognitive focus, and their creative confidence beliefs. They found that students with higher engagement were more likely to have stronger creativity perceptions.

In addition, several studies have reported the mediating effects of engagement on the asso- ciation between students’ digital/media experience and their creativity development. For instance, Malik et al. (2020) collected survey data from 334 undergraduate students in Chinese universities and found that their intrinsic motivation, representing their emotional engagement, mediated

the association between digital inquiry-related behavior and creativity. Likewise, Sun (2020) conducted a survey of 652 undergraduate students in Chinese public universities and found that the students’ cognitive engagement (i.e., time- and energy-related efforts) partially mediated the relationship between digital inquiry-related behavior and self-reported creativity. These studies suggest that both emotional engagement and cognitive engagement play mediating roles in the relationship between perceived digital inquiry and creativity.

Although researchers have reported that perceived digital inquiry has strong associations with emotional and cognitive engagement (Chiu & Churchill, [2015;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2020;](#disclosure-statement) Marty et al., 2013; Wu & Wu, 2020) and these associations can foster perceived creativity (Álvarez-Huerta et al., [2021;](#disclosure-statement) Hwang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022), few studies have examined the relationships between the engagement components of the TME in authentic educational practice. It is import- ant to investigate the associations between these variables (i.e., engagement dispositions, acts, and benefits) from the perspectives of theoretical application and development. The aim of this study was to investigate these associations.

Based on the studies described above, the following hypotheses are proposed (see Figure 2 for a visual representation):

- H1: There is a positive association between perceived digital inquiry and emotional engagement.
- H2: There is a positive association between perceived digital inquiry and cognitive engagement.
- H3: There is a positive association between perceived digital inquiry and perceived creativity.
- H4: There is a bidirectional association between emotional engagement and cognitive engagement.
- H5: There is a positive association between emotional engagement and perceived creativity.
- H6: There is a positive association between cognitive engagement and perceived creativity.
- H7: Perceived digital inquiry is positively associated with perceived creativity via emotional engagement.
- H8: Perceived digital inquiry is positively associated with perceived creativity via cognitive engagement.

##  Methodology 

### _Research design and participants_

This study used a self-reported questionnaire to collect data. We recruited 336 students from three Hong Kong secondary schools. The schools were purposely selected from 31 schools that 

436 X. WENG AND T. K. F. CHIU

participated in a cross-sector STEM collaborative project of the local government, universities, and secondary schools. Our selection criteria were (1) the schools should have similar academic backgrounds with average learning performance in the Hong Kong education context; (2) the teachers should have STEM educational backgrounds and receive teaching qualification in math- ematics, science, or computer science; and (3) the schools should teach all students STEM using digital making activities, such as Scratch coding, traffic light system design or smart home design activities using Arduino Kits and Microbits. The STEM digital making programs were integrated into existing technology curricula in the schools. In addition to providing financial support and professional development for the teachers to conduct STEM digital making activities, the edu- cation experts from the government, and two STEM education professors have formed a panel to guide and evaluate the project implementation in the schools. We finally received 311 ques- tionnaires (a response rate of 92.6%) from the selected schools. After removing questionnaires with missing values, 166 responses were retained from school A (Grade 2, female: n = 71; male: n = 95), 56 from school B (Grade 1, female: n = 22; male: n = 34), and 83 from school C (Grade 1, female: n = 43; male: n = 40), for a total of 305 for analysis. Males accounted for 55.4% of the sample (n = 169) and females for 44.6% (n = 136). All the students are Chinese.

### _Measures in the questionnaire_

The first part of the questionnaire collected demographic information such as the students’ gender and school name. The second part consisted of items investigating perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity.

The questionnaire included four measures, all of which were measured using 5-point Likert scale items. The reliability and validity of the items are specified below. All the items were translated into Chinese and checked by three teachers from the participating schools to ensure that they were readable and understandable.

The measure of perceived digital inquiry was evaluated using items adapted from a study by Ng ( 2012), who used self-perception measures to explore students’ digital literacy, with original Cronbach’s alpha values α = .88, including acceptable reliability. These items were tested in the study of the Chiu ([2022)](#disclosure-statement) and Chiu et al. ([2022)](#disclosure-statement) with similar background participants. They were modified to fit the context of STEM education. The items for this dimension were “I am able to use technology to test scientific explanations in my STEM project,” “I am able to search and combine various Internet resources to conduct scientific investigations,” and “I am able to use different technologies to research scientific topics”.

The measures of emotional engagement were evaluated using items adapted from the study of Skinner et al. ( 2009), with acceptable reliability (α = . 82). The items were tested in the study of the Chiu ([2022)](#disclosure-statement) and Chiu et al. ([2022)](#disclosure-statement) with similar background participants who had taken part in online learning from different aspects. They were modified to fit our STEM education context. The items for emotional engagement were “When doing STEM projects, I feel like I’m doing something important to me,” “I love having more time to work on my STEM projects,” and “I like to use my free time to think about my STEM projects”. Moreover, the items for cognitive engagement were adapted from Wang et al. (2022) that validated and verified the items to measure high school students’ cognitive engagement in science and mathematics, with accept- able reliability (α \> .75). The items fitted our participants’ education level and subject domains and were tested in the Hong Kong context (Chiu, [2022;](#disclosure-statement) Chiu et al., [2022)](#disclosure-statement). They were “I am able to participate in different types of learning activities to make a good STEM project,” “I am able to complete the tasks planned for the STEM project promptly,” and “I am able to enrich my knowledge by talking to other people about STEM projects”.

The measure of perceived creativity was evaluated using items adapted from a study by Tan et al. ( 2008), who investigated students’ creativity self-efficacy, with α =.80 (i.e., acceptable reliability). We adapted the items for our STEM education context. The items for this dimen- sion were “I am able to come up with some innovative approaches or questions,” “I can apply 

JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON TECHNOLOGY IN EDUCATION 437

what I know in unknown situations,” and “I can find new ideas from the information when others are not inspired”.

###  _Data collection procedure_

We obtained the participants’ consent before distributing the two-part questionnaire. The ques- tionnaire was distributed to the participants via an online platform with the help of the STEM subject coordinators of the schools. The students were asked to submit a completed questionnaire to the researcher within one week after it was distributed. The coordinators reminded the par- ticipants to respond to the items with close attention and to answer all the questions.

##  Results 

### _Construct validity and reliability_

This study is the first to adapt a scale involving the different perceived competencies and engagement acts of STEM digital learners to the Hong Kong context. We tested whether the factor loadings were consistent to validate their use in this context.

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using maximum likelihood estimation in Mplus 8.3 was used to verify the scale structure and check whether the data were a satisfactory fit for the measurement model. Various indices were used to evaluate the overall model fit (Hair, 2010 ). The goodness-of-fit statistics for the scale suggested that the four-factor model fitted the data well (χ2 = 118.82, df = 48, χ2/df = 2.48, CFI = .98, TLI = .97, SRMR = .02, RMSEA = .07). The items’ factor loadings ranged from .57 to .80. As shown in Table 1, the Cronbach’s alpha values of the four factors were .89 (perceived digital inquiry), .90 (emotional engagement), .88 (cognitive engagement), and .91 (perceived creativity), indicating good internal consistency.

### _Descriptive and correlation analyses_

The descriptive statistics for the four factors examined are presented in [Table 1.](#data-collection-procedure) Perceived creativity (M = 3.75, SD = .75) scored the highest among all the factors. Emotional engagement (M = 3.67, SD = .75) had the lowest score. The mean score and standard deviation for cognitive engagement were 

3.73 and .71, respectively, and those for perceived digital inquiry were 3.72 and .73. The correlation matrix of the four factors is shown in [Table 1.](#data-collection-procedure) There were significant positive 

correlations between perceived digital inquiry and emotional engagement (r = .78, _p_ \< .01), cognitive engagement (r = .85, _p_ \< .01), and perceived creativity (r = .80, _p_ \< .01); emotional engagement and cognitive engagement (r = .81, _p_ \< .01) and perceived creativity (r = .80, _p_ \< .01); and cognitive engagement and perceived creativity (r = .77, _p_ \< .01).

###  _Mediation analysis_

We further investigated the direct and indirect relationships between different variables using structural equation modeling (SEM). Perceived digital inquiry was the exogenous variable in the proposed model (see [Figure 2)](#methodology), and emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived

creativity were the endogenous variables. In the analysis, all the variables were standardized to minimize potential bias caused by the wide range of variances. We adopted a 95% confidence interval (CI) with 1,000 bootstrap samples to assess statistical significance.

The analysis revealed that perceived digital inquiry had significant positive direct effects on emotional engagement (β = 0.87, _p_ \< 0.001, 95% CI \[0.79, 0.95\]) and cognitive engagement (β = 0.95, _p_\< 0.001, 95% CI \[0.91, 0.99\]). However, the effect of perceived digital inquiry on perceived creativity was not significant (β = 0.77, _p_ \> 0.05, 95% CI \[0.25, 3.03\]). Therefore, the results sup- ported H1 and H2, but H3 was rejected. The analysis also revealed a significant positive bidi- rectional association between emotional engagement and cognitive engagement (β = 0.54, _p_ \< 0.01, 95% CI \[0.16, 0.87\]), supporting H4. Furthermore, we found that emotional engagement had significant positive direct effects on perceived creativity (β = 0.58, _p_\< 0.05, 95% CI \[0.20, 1.65\]), but cognitive engagement did not have a significant effect on perceived creativity (β = −0.41, _p_\> 0.05, 95% CI \[-1.76, 0.66\]). Correspondingly, H5 was supported and H6 was rejected. The direct and indirect relationships between the variables are shown in Table 2 . 

Additionally, the analysis revealed a significant indirect effect of perceived digital inquiry on perceived creativity through emotional engagement (β = 0.51, _p_ \< 0.05, 95% CI \[0.18, 1.55\]). However, the pathway from perceived digital inquiry via cognitive engagement to perceived creativity was not significant (β = −0.39, _p_ \> 0.05, 95% CI \[-1.75, 0.61\]). Therefore, H7 was supported and H8 was rejected.

Overall, significant direct main effects were found between the four variables, except the associations between perceived digital inquiry and creativity and between cognitive engagement and perceived creativity (see [Table 2)](#discussion). The total effect from perceived digital inquiry to creativity was significant (β = 0.88, _p \<_0.001, 95% CI \[0.82, 0.95\]). These findings suggest that emotional engagement has a partial mediating effect on the relationship between perceived digital inquiry and creativity.

##  Discussion

The two primary goals of this study were (i) to examine the direct associations between perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity and (ii) to apply the TME to investigate whether emotional engagement and cognitive engagement had indirect effects on the relationship between perceived digital inquiry and creativity. We used SEM to examine the mediating effects of emotional and cognitive engagement in our proposed model.

The results have a major theoretical contribution. They provided more empirical evidence to support Lawson and Lawson’s (2013) relatively new conceptual framework of student engage- ment—TME—by presenting the significant relationships that exist among acts of engagement, benefits from engagement, and dispositions for engagement in STEM education. This study supported the application of TME in student STEM learning. We encourage more applications of TME in other learning environments to reveal or explain the interactions between students’ digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and creativity.

JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON TECHNOLOGY IN EDUCATION 439

The results also have the following empirical implications. They showed that perceived digital inquiry had direct positive associations with both emotional engagement and cognitive engage- ment (H1 and H2). These findings align with previous results showing that perceived inquiry-related features can indicate a disposition that triggers different engagement acts (Wu & Wu, 2020). Students who perceive stronger digital inquiry tend to try out their skills by actively engaging in learning activities emotionally and cognitively (Porat et al., 2018). Moreover, our results indi- cate that the direct association between perceived digital inquiry and creativity is not statistically significant (H3). This finding is inconsistent with that of Hwang et al. (2018), who reported a significant positive correlation between students’ perceptions of inquiry-related mobile adoption and creativity tendency. This suggests that students’ development of creativity depends on their engagement with a task. Compared with students who engage in STEM activities, disengaged students are less likely to feel that they can create something new.

A significant positive bidirectional association between emotional engagement and cognitive engagement was identified (H4). This finding aligns with reports of interactions between the two types of engagement (Chiu, 2021, 2022; Chiu et al., 2012, 2022; Dubovi & Tabak, 2021; Hong et al., 2020). Emotional engagement encourages cognitive engagement development, and vice versa. Correspondingly, we included the interaction between different engagement acts as a factor influ- encing engagement development, supplementary to the suggestion of Fredricks et al. ( 2004 ) that the interaction between the individual and the context affects student engagement.

Furthermore, emotional engagement had a significant positive effect on perceived creativity (H5). This result supports reports that emotional engagement makes a notable contribution to creativity development (Wang et al., 2022). Being emotionally engaged in a learning activity means that students are devoting their affection resources to the tasks, which will foster their perceptions of competencies such as creativity. However, we did not find a statistically significant association between cognitive engagement and perceived creativity (H6). This finding is incon- sistent with studies that reported a significant positive correlation between these two variables (Álvarez-Huerta et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). The discrepancy may be because students with strong cognitive engagement in STEM digital making activities are more likely to feel challenged or frustrated. A challenging experience with a heavy cognitive load could lead students to per- ceive their competencies negatively as a result of cognitive overload and frustration (Chiu & Churchill, 2015; Reynolds & Caperton, 2011). This finding indicates the need for educators to carefully design learning tasks with appropriate difficulty levels for students. It can avoid the possible negative effects that may be caused by cognitive overload.

We next examined the indirect relationships between the variables. We found an indirect effect of emotional engagement on the relationship between perceived digital inquiry and cre- ativity, supporting H7. This result aligns with the finding of Malik et al. (2020) that emotional engagement mediates the association between students’ digital inquiry related to behavior and creativity. As a direct association between perceived digital inquiry and perceived creativity was not found in the present study, this mediation effect suggests an alternative approach to pro- moting perceived creativity by developing students’ emotional engagement. Nevertheless, it is notable that there was no indirect effect of cognitive engagement on the relationship between perceived digital inquiry and creativity (H8). The result is inconsistent with Sun’s (2020) con- clusion that cognitive engagement can partially mediate the relationship between digital inquiry-related behavior and students’ creativity. A possible reason for this inconsistency is that the contradictory relationship between cognitive engagement and perceived creativity caused by cognitive load (Reynolds & Caperton, 2011) may eliminate the mediating effect of cognitive engagement on the association between perceived digital inquiry and creativity. Another potential explanation is that in STEM education, making creative outcomes requires long-term investment. Interest and joy would encourage students to invest in learning for a longer period. The user-friendly digital making platforms adopted, including Scratch, Arduino Kits, and Microbits, were designed to foster learners’ interest and joy in digital making. They can be promising tools to promote student creativity in STEM learning.

440 X. WENG AND T. K. F. CHIU

Overall, our results show that in secondary school STEM education, perceived digital inquiry can be an important personal resource that directly improves students’ emotional and cognitive engagement. Moreover, emotional engagement can mediate the positive relationship between perceived digital inquiry and perceived creativity. Therefore, interventions aimed at fostering perceived digital inquiry may be useful for developing self-perceived creativity of secondary school STEM learners. We recommend that teachers should make efforts to emotionally engage students in digital inquiry activities when the learning objective is creativity (Chiu et al., 2020; Weng, Chiu, & Jong, 2022; Weng, Cui, et al., 2022). The more emotionally engaged students feel with their learning tasks, the more likely it is that they will feel that they can create some- thing new.

Our findings provide two practical suggestions for fostering creativity in digital-supported STEM learning. The first suggestion is that STEM teachers can apply different strategies to make students feel more engaged in utilizing digital tools for inquiry-based learning. For example, they could use various digital making platforms and tools to encourage students to complete small projects. The second suggestion is that instead of emphasizing STEM disciplinary knowledge development, STEM teachers are encouraged to enhance students’ STEM interest and identity first before STEM learning. This enhanced affection would lead to greater emotional engagement. The students would sustain their STEM digital inquiry learning for more creative work. To achieve the desired outcomes, the teachers could share some alumni’s success stories of STEM learning, and show the interesting and inspiring STEM products.

## Conclusion, limitations, and future directions

This study investigated the direct relationships between perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity, and the indirect effects of emotional engagement and cognitive engagement on the association between perceived digital inquiry and creativity. The results imply that STEM digital making activities show promise for promoting students’ perceived competencies and learning engagement.

However, this study has some limitations. First, we cannot infer causal relationships between the variables because of the cross-sectional research design. Besides, because the number of participants was relatively small, the research findings should be confirmed by studies with a larger sample size. Moreover, other types of data sources such as qualitative interviews or class- room observations should be collected to enhance the explanatory power of the study. Additionally, each of the four variables was evaluated using only three items. As the dimensions involved are complex, it is unclear whether the measurements satisfactorily reflect these four variables. Furthermore, the measurements were self-reported, so the relationships between perceived cre- ativity and the other variables may have been inflated or deflated. Nevertheless, the CFA indicated that four separate factors were derived from the constructs. Despite these limitations, by following a TME framework, this study provides the first evidence of the interactions between secondary STEM learners’ perceived competencies and their engagement.

This programme was designed to enhance perceived digital inquiry holistically in line with self-perception theory (Teng, 2018). The adoption of digital tools, scientific inquiry, and hands-on experience obtained through digital making activities foster students’ competencies and learning engagement (Stork, 2020). Accordingly, future studies could evaluate the out- comes and report students’ feedback on the digital making programme in terms of develop- ments in their self-perceived competencies and learning engagement. Furthermore, future research could use other frameworks to investigate the associations between student perceived digital inquiry, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, and perceived creativity in STEM digital making environments. Future studies can also be conducted in other learning contexts, such as an Artificial Intelligence-facilitated learning environment instead of a STEM-based environment.
